findings.headline: Ashbourne Reborn regeneration project carries high assessed risk despite being on track
findings.detail: A £15.2m capital regeneration scheme (Ashbourne Reborn, funded via Levelling Up) is being managed by the council as the Accountable Body. The council has assessed the risks as 'high' and is managing them through nominated officers and finance staff liaison to ensure grant claims are accurate and timely. The project is on track for completion in 2026/27.
findings.matters: A £15.2m capital scheme that is the council's responsibility as Accountable Body carries concentration risk. High assessed risk means the council has identified material things that could go wrong. If the project slips or faces cost overruns, it could impact the council's balance sheet and reserves.
findings.figures: £15.2m capital project; project completion scheduled for 2026/27
findings.quote: There are risks associated with the Accountable Body status for the Ashbourne Reborn Levelling Up scheme, which is a £15.2m capital project to regenerate Ashbourne town centre. These risks are significant and have been assessed as 'high'.

findings.headline: Monitoring Officer resigned during 2025/26; recruitment ongoing with interim arrangements in place
findings.detail: The council's Monitoring Officer—a statutory role responsible for ensuring lawfulness and ethical standards—resigned during the financial year. Interim arrangements have been put in place while recruitment proceeds. This is a key governance role with personal statutory duties.
findings.matters: The Monitoring Officer role is critical to ensuring the council operates within law and maintains governance standards. A vacant statutory post creates execution risk on compliance and ethics oversight. The longer the interim period, the greater the residual risk.
findings.figures: Monitoring Officer role vacant during 2025/26; recruitment ongoing
findings.quote: The Council's Monitoring Officer resigned during 2025/26, and interim arrangements were put in place while recruitment takes place.

findings.headline: Council tax and business rates collection rates fell below target in 2025/26, driven by cost of living crisis
findings.detail: The revenues and benefits service, delivered by Chesterfield Borough Council, achieved all KPIs in 2025/26 except for council tax collection (in-year and prior year) and non-domestic rates (in-year). These underperformed their targets. The statement attributes this to the cost of living crisis and notes that recovery action is continuing.
findings.matters: Collection rates directly affect the income available to fund services and close the budget gap. Falling rates in a cost-of-living crisis environment suggest the underlying trend may worsen before it improves, worsening the financial sustainability picture.
findings.figures: Council tax (in-year and prior year) collection and non-domestic rates (in-year) collection: slightly under target
findings.quote: In 2025/26 Chesterfield Borough Council achieved all the key performance indicators in the Revenues and Benefits contract, except for those relating to in-year and prior year collection of council tax and in-year collection of non-domestic rates, which were slightly under target. Payments have been impacted by the 'cost of living' crisis. Recovery action is continuing.

findings.headline: Significant budget gap in future years with no savings plan yet in place
findings.detail: The council has balanced the 2026/27 budget but faces a significant budget gap in future years identified in the Medium-Term Financial Plan. The statement explicitly identifies this as a significant governance issue and requires a savings plan to be developed by November 2026, with an updated MTFP and balanced budget for 2027/28 by March 2027. As of the statement date, this plan does not yet exist.
findings.matters: A council that cannot project a path to financial sustainability is a credit risk. The gap is material enough to be flagged as a governance issue, and the extended timeline to address it (not until March 2027) means there is no current plan for closing it.
findings.figures: Significant budget gap identified for future years; balanced budget set for 2026/27 only
findings.quote: The Council's Medium-Term Financial Plan identifies a significant budget gap in future years. To mitigate this risk, the Council has a Medium-Term Financial Strategy and Medium-Term Financial Plan in place. A balanced budget has been set for 2026/27, However, a savings plan must be developed to show how the Authority plans to address the budget gap for future years. This has been identified as a significant governance issue.

findings.paper_title: 1a Internal Audit Annual Report 2025.26 Appendix 1 v2
findings.headline: Assurance and Monitoring weaknesses account for 36% (21 of 59) of all audit recommendations, indicating widespread failure to oversee controls.
findings.detail: Of 59 audit recommendations across 2025/26, 21 stem from Assurance & Monitoring failures—defined as unclear responsibility for checking, not identifying or acting on recurring problems, checking the wrong things, or under-sampling. This is the dominant root cause category by far, suggesting controls exist but are not being verified or overseen properly.
findings.matters: Controls that are not monitored are controls that may be silently failing. A 36% concentration in monitoring failures means the council has weak oversight of its financial and operational controls, increasing the risk of undetected errors or fraud.
findings.figures: Assurance & Monitoring: 21 recommendations out of 59 total (36%)
findings.quote: Root Cause Number of Recommendations % Assurance & Monitoring 21 36

findings.paper_title: 1a Internal Audit Annual Report 2025.26 Appendix 1 v2
findings.headline: Grants to Voluntary and Community Organisations received Limited Assurance on first audit, indicating weak controls over discretionary grants.
findings.detail: Grants to Voluntary and Community Organisations is a new audit receiving Limited Assurance, meaning controls over how grants are awarded, monitored and accounted for are either missing or ineffective. The council cannot be confident that grant spending achieves its intended objectives or complies with requirements.
findings.matters: Poor grant controls create exposure to misuse of public money, non-compliance with funding conditions, and potential clawback of external grants. Lenders and auditors scrutinise weak grant governance as a sign of broader control failure.
findings.figures: Grants to Voluntary and Community Organisations: Limited Assurance (new audit)
findings.quote: Grants to Voluntary and Community Organisations Limited New

findings.paper_title: 1a Internal Audit Annual Report 2025.26 Appendix 1 v2
findings.headline: Housing Rents and Housing Contract Compliance received Limited Assurance on first audit, indicating new control weaknesses in the council's housing stock management.
findings.detail: Housing Rents and Housing Contract Compliance is a new audit area in 2025/26 and immediately received Limited Assurance, the lowest passing grade. Limited Assurance means certain important controls are either not in place or not operating effectively, creating risk that the system may not achieve its objectives. This is the council's first formal assessment of this area.
findings.matters: Housing income is a material revenue stream for councils, and control weaknesses in rent collection and contract compliance expose the council to revenue loss and financial mismanagement. This is a red flag for lenders on municipal housing viability.
findings.figures: Housing Rents and Housing Contract Compliance: Limited Assurance (new audit in 2025/26)
findings.quote: Housing Rents and Housing Contract Limited New

findings.paper_title: 1a Internal Audit Annual Report 2025.26 Appendix 1 v2
findings.headline: Substantial assurance audits fell from 28% to 14% of the portfolio, a significant drop in control quality.
findings.detail: In 2024/25, five audits received Substantial Assurance (28% of 18 audits). In 2025/26, only two audits received Substantial Assurance (14% of 14 audits). Conversely, Reasonable Assurance audits increased from 61% to 72%. This shift indicates a broad weakening of control environments across the council's operations.
findings.matters: Declining assurance levels suggest the council's control framework is deteriorating, increasing risk to financial management and compliance. Lenders rely on strong internal controls to manage council finances.
findings.figures: Substantial Assurance: 5 (28%) in 2024/25 vs 2 (14%) in 2025/26. Reasonable Assurance: 11 (61%) in 2024/25 vs 10 (72%) in 2025/26.
findings.quote: Assurance Level 2024/25 Number 2024/25 % 2025/26 Number 2025/26 % Substantial 5 28 2 14 Reasonable 11 61 10 72

findings.headline: Significant unforeseen repair costs signalling asset condition issues
findings.detail: Repairs and maintenance budget exceeded by £97k due to significant unforeseen work at multiple locations including Town Hall, Northwood Depot and Bakewell riverbank. The report acknowledges this is a reactive budget and flags that further review is needed to ensure adequate resource allocation.
findings.matters: Reactive maintenance pressures indicate aging assets in poor condition, which may require substantial capital investment ahead.
findings.figures: £97k repairs overspend
findings.quote: The repairs and maintenance budget is forecast to exceed budget by £97k as a result of significant unforeseen repair and maintenance work at numerous locations across the District, including the Town Hall, Northwood Depot and Bakewell riverbank. It is acknowledged that the repairs and maintenance budget is a reactive one and further review of this budget is to take place to ensure adequate budget resource is allocated.

findings.headline: Investment income overspend dependent on interest rates staying above budget assumptions
findings.detail: The council is forecasting £364k overachievement of investment income because base rates have remained higher than the 3.5% assumption made when the budget was set. However, the report notes this forecast 'is based on a number of assumptions and will continue to be refined throughout the financial year', and rates have already started falling (now 3.75% vs 3.5% budgeted).
findings.matters: A key driver of the reported underspend is rate-sensitive income that could reverse if base rates fall further, which would expose underlying structural deficits more quickly.
findings.figures: £364k investment income overachievement; base rate now 3.75% vs 3.5% budgeted
findings.quote: The base rate has subsequently reduced to 4% on 7th August and again to 3.75% on 17th December 2025, but as this is still over and above the budgeted base rate the Council continues to receive better returns on investments than anticipated.

findings.headline: Council explicitly warns of high-risk financial pressures from 2027/28 onwards
findings.detail: The Strategic Risk Register identifies Financial Resilience as high risk, pending delivery of required savings. The report states that significant financial challenges have been highlighted in the MTFP from 2027/28 onwards, and the council is creating a new Financial Sustainability Reserve to manage the transition. The report emphasises that creation of this reserve 'does not remove the underlying financial pressures' and that 'a comprehensive and sustainable savings programme will need to be developed and delivered'.
findings.matters: This is the council explicitly warning that structural deficits are forecast and that achieving balance will require major savings in the medium term, which is a core lender concern.
findings.figures: £1,221,081 forecast underspend being transferred to Financial Sustainability Reserve
findings.quote: Financial Resilience has been identified on the Council's Strategic Risk Register and has been assessed as high risk, pending the delivery of the required savings due to the outcome of the Local Government Finance Settlement for 2026/27 and beyond.

findings.headline: Waste service delivery failures driving income compensation
findings.detail: The council is forecasting £258k additional income from waste default notices, described as resulting from 'continuing route optimisation service deficiencies'. The report explicitly flags this as an ongoing issue that has been built into the 2026/27 budget, indicating a persistent operational problem.
findings.matters: The council is relying on penalty income to offset service delivery failures, which is financially fragile and signals operational risk.
findings.figures: £258k additional income from waste default notices
findings.quote: an additional £258k income will be achieved through waste default notices because of continuing route optimisation service deficiencies. This is considered to be an ongoing issue, and provision has been made for additional income in the revenue budget for 2026/27 onwards.

findings.headline: Structural income losses locked into future budgets
findings.detail: Car parking income is down £35k permanently due to the 30 minutes free parking policy, and recycling credits are down £59k due to material market conditions. Both are described as ongoing reductions and have been built into the 2026/27 budget. This means future budgets start from a lower baseline.
findings.matters: These represent permanent revenue reductions that will constrain the council's financial flexibility going forward.
findings.figures: £35k car parking underspend, £59k recycling credits reduction
findings.quote: This pressure is anticipated to be a permanent reduction in car parking income and therefore has been included in the medium-term financial plan approved by Council on 5th March 2026.

findings.paper_title: 1. Supplementary budget to support microsme businesses and communities Council 5march2026
findings.headline: Council acknowledges forecast funding gaps and potential need for savings from 2027/28 onwards, the period when this grant commitment is active.
findings.detail: The report explicitly warns that the council has forecast funding gaps and may need to identify savings starting in 2027/28. The council notes it may also need to use reserves further to manage timing differences in savings delivery. These warnings apply while the council is committing to fund ongoing grant schemes with reserve drawdowns.
findings.matters: The council is signalling financial stress and uncertainty about its ability to maintain discretionary spending, raising questions about the durability of this two-year funding commitment.
findings.figures: Savings requirements potential 2027/28 onwards; no specific amounts quantified in this paper
findings.quote: The potential need to identify savings in 2027/28 onwards, alongside the potential further use of reserves to manage timing differences in savings delivery

findings.paper_title: 1. Supplementary budget to support microsme businesses and communities Council 5march2026
findings.headline: Council is drawing £300,000 from reserves for ongoing discretionary spending, rated medium risk due to forecast budget gaps.
findings.detail: The council proposes using reserves totalling £300,000 (£150,000 per year for 2026-27 and 2027-28) to continue grant schemes. The council explicitly rates this as medium risk, stating that ordinarily the risk would be low, but forecast funding gaps mean future savings requirements cannot be ruled out. The council may need to use reserves further to manage timing of savings delivery.
findings.matters: Using reserves for ongoing spending rather than capital investment or one-off costs, while expecting budget gaps, suggests financial stress and potential vulnerability of these programmes to future cuts.
findings.figures: £300,000 over two years (£150,000 each year); funded from Economic Development reserve £138,181, Corporate Plan priorities reserve £109,499, committed expenditure reserve £23,049, grants unapplied reserve £9,271, salary underspend transfer £20,000
findings.quote: While the financial risk associated with this proposal would ordinarily be considered low, the Council's forecast funding gaps mean that future savings requirements cannot be ruled out

findings.paper_title: 1. Supplementary budget to support microsme businesses and communities Council 5march2026
findings.headline: Government funding for business and community grants ends 31 March 2026, forcing the council to self-fund or discontinue programmes.
findings.detail: The council received £3.7m in UKSPF and REPF funding from 2023-2026, which primarily funded Rural Innovation Grants for businesses (£1.4m) and Community Resilience Grants (£525k). From April 2026, no external funding will be available. EMCCA has confirmed it will not provide capital grant funding for the foreseeable future, leaving the council to choose between self-funding these programmes or ceasing them.
findings.matters: Withdrawal of external funding forces difficult choices about discretionary spending when the council simultaneously faces forecast budget gaps.
findings.figures: £3,723,835 UKSPF/REPF received 2023-2026; £1.4m via Rural Innovation Grants to 118 businesses, £525,300 via Community Resilience Grants to 47 communities
findings.quote: External funding for business Rural Innovation Grants and local Community Resilience Grants was previously provided by the Government (via UK Shared Prosperity Fund) and latterly via EMCCA, but ceases totally on 31 March 2026.

findings.headline: Treasury investment balance projected to decline 61% from £12.8m to £5.0m through 2029
findings.detail: The council's treasury investments are forecast to fall from £12.8m at 31 March 2026 to £5.0m by 31 March 2029, representing a significant reduction in liquid resources over a three-year period. The strategy attributes this decline to the medium-term financial plan but does not specify the underlying drivers within this document.
findings.matters: Declining reserves reduce the council's financial buffer and flexibility to manage unexpected pressures or revenue shortfalls without increased borrowing or service cuts
findings.quote: expenditure and reserves are predicted to fall as per the medium-term financial plan elsewhere on this agenda

findings.headline: Income from fees and charges totals £8.8m (37% of all revenue income in 2026/27), with car parking and waste charges alone representing 74% of this income stream
findings.detail: The council's revenue income is heavily dependent on discretionary fees and charges: £8.8m forecast in 2026/27, which is 37% of total income—more than council tax. Of this, car parking generates £3m and waste collection (including recycling credits) £3.5m. This concentration of income from discretionary services and volatile waste markets exposes the council to demand shocks, particularly if a cost-of-living crisis reduces parking usage or recyclate values fall.
findings.matters: A council where over one-third of revenue depends on discretionary economic activity is exposed to recession and cost-of-living impacts outside its control. A 10-15% drop in parking or waste income would immediately trigger budget shortfalls in years already forecasting major deficits.
findings.figures: £8.8m total (37% of all income); £3.0m car parking; £3.5m waste (combined 74% of fees income)
findings.quote: The most significant sources of income from fees and charges forecast for 2026/27 are car parking £3m and waste collection (including recycling credits) £3.5m.

findings.headline: Waste collection vehicles need replacement but only £1.5m is reserved against a historic replacement cost of £3.6m, creating an underfunded capital liability
findings.detail: The council's waste collection vehicles acquired in 2020/21 and 2021/22 at a cost of £3.6m will require replacement within the MTFS period. A dedicated reserve has been established and is forecast to hold £1.5m by 31 March 2027, but the council acknowledges this is insufficient. The paper notes annual revenue contributions should be made 'if affordable' to build the reserve, but affordability is highly doubtful given the forecast budget deficits.
findings.matters: A significant known capital liability is only 42% funded, requiring either immediate borrowing, further reserve drawdown, or deferral of replacement. In a council facing major revenue deficits, this is a timing risk that could force difficult trade-offs between revenue and capital commitments.
findings.figures: £3.6m (historic vehicle acquisition cost), £1.5m (reserve balance forecast 31 Mar 2027)
findings.quote: The current vehicles were acquired in 2020/21 and 2021/22 at a cost of £3.6m.

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation is scheduled for April 2028 with no financial provision beyond £50,000, while other councils estimate £17m in pre-vesting costs
findings.detail: The government has announced LGR for Derbyshire with vesting in April 2028. The council has only included £50,000 in 2026/27 for project management costs. Other Derbyshire councils' combined case for change estimates £17m in total pre-vesting implementation costs, but no decision has been made on the preferred structural option (decision expected summer 2026). Actual contributions required from each council remain unknown.
findings.matters: LGR creates undefined budget exposure in 2027/28 and 2028/29, precisely when the council is forecasting major deficits (£2.8m-£4.2m). If the council must fund material transition costs during this period, it may force more severe financial action than currently planned.
findings.figures: £50,000 (2026/27 only); £17m (other councils' total pre-vesting estimates)
findings.quote: The case for change submitted by the other Derbyshire districts, boroughs and Derby City Council indicates that implementation costs would begin to arise from 2026/27, with total pre-vesting costs estimated at £17 million.

findings.headline: Strategic reserves are forecast to fall from £12.3m to £7.3m by 2031 (41% reduction), primarily to fund capital spending and close budget gaps
findings.detail: The council's strategic reserves (earmarked for specific purposes including capital replacement and contingency) fall from £12.3m (31 March 2026) to £8.5m (31 March 2027) and £7.3m (31 March 2031). This depletion is driven by using reserves to finance the capital programme and to meet revenue budget gaps. The Director of Resources explicitly notes 'higher levels of reserves are required in the medium-term to improve financial resilience.'
findings.matters: Declining reserves indicate a council consuming its financial buffers rather than operating sustainably. This reduces flexibility to handle unexpected costs or revenue shortfalls, and mirrors the pattern seen in councils that have issued Section 114 notices.
findings.quote: Strategic reserves are estimated to total £12.3 million at 31st March 2026, reducing to £8.5 million at 31st March 2027 and £7.3m by 31st March 2031.

findings.headline: The council depends on an £820,000 Extended Producer Responsibility grant in 2026/27 that the council flags as 'high financial risk' and assumes will reduce to zero by 2029/30
findings.detail: Outside the main settlement, the council received an £820k grant for waste management under the Extended Producer Responsibility scheme. This grant has been essential to balancing the 2026/27 budget. However, the council explicitly flags this as a high financial risk, has no certainty of its continuation, and the financial plan assumes it reduces to zero over the period to 2029/30. Loss of this income mid-cycle would immediately create an additional deficit.
findings.matters: A council dependent on temporary, unconfirmed grant funding for budget balance is exposed to sudden deficits outside its control. This signals vulnerability to government policy changes and reduces financial predictability.
findings.quote: There is a high financial risk that this grant may not be available in future years or that it will reduce significantly. The MTFP assumes that it will reduce to zero over the period 2026/27 to 2029/30.

findings.headline: Business rates baseline reset in 2026/27 permanently cuts the council's retained business rates income from £4.0m to £1.5m, a 62% reduction
findings.detail: As part of the Fair Funding Review, the government fully reset the business rates baseline from 2026/27. This technical change reduced how much business rates Derbyshire Dales can retain. The council's business rates income falls from £3.95m (2024/25) to £1.13m (2026/27). This is described as having 'very significant impact' and is one of the primary drivers of the forecast budget deficits.
findings.matters: This represents a permanent £2.8m annual loss of a council's most controllable own-source revenue, making it increasingly dependent on council tax (68% by 2028/29) and temporary government grants. It signals reduced financial autonomy and indicates the council's sustainable income base has shrunk.
findings.figures: £3.95m (2024/25) to £1.13m (2026/27); Business rates share of funding drops from 29.7% to 8.5%
findings.quote: a reset of the baseline for retained business rates in full in 2026/27

findings.headline: Budget deficits escalate from £0.7m in 2027/28 to £4.2m in 2029/30, with savings described as 'extremely challenging' to find
findings.detail: After balancing 2026/27 through reserve use and grants, the forecasts show: £0.7m deficit in 2027/28 (noted as 'challenging'), £2.8m in 2028/29, and £4.2m in 2029/30 (after transitional protections end). The council states balancing the budget beyond 2027/28 will be 'extremely challenging' and acknowledges it will face 'difficult decisions' during 2026/27 to find these savings.
findings.matters: This trajectory indicates the council is unlikely to find £4.2m in annual sustainable savings without material service reductions, asset disposals, or increased borrowing. For a lender, this signals growing financial stress and limited flexibility.
findings.quote: there is a need to identify significant further savings or additional income of £0.7m in 2027/28, rising to £2.8m in 2028/29 and £4.2m in 2029/30

findings.headline: Transitional government funding protection ends abruptly in 2029/30, creating a sudden £1.2m budget gap
findings.detail: The council receives transitional grants to cushion the impact of the 2026 funding reforms: £333k in 2026/27, rising to £1.25m in 2028/29. However, the paper flags no certainty these protections will continue beyond 2028/29. When they end, the council loses approximately 10% of external funding in a single year unless it has made preemptive savings.
findings.matters: A sudden loss of £1.2m funding in 2029/30 would require either severe service cuts or significant borrowing mid-loan term, materially changing the council's financial profile and debt servicing capacity.
findings.quote: When the transitional protections end in 2029/30, the budget gap will increase by £1.2m unless savings have been made in the meantime.

findings.paper_title: 3. Capital Programme Update Quarter 3 March Council meeting
findings.headline: Warm Homes Grant allocation cut 38% in year one (£50k reduction) due to procurement delays
findings.detail: The first-year allocation for the Warm Homes Grant scheme has been cut from £130,000 to £80,000 due to 'delays in procurement'. The council notes the allocation 'could be reduced further if delivery is delayed'. Years 2 and 3 remain at £500,000 each but are at risk if these delivery challenges persist.
findings.matters: This shows the council is failing to deploy external grant funding as planned due to delivery and procurement capacity constraints. This pattern could affect other grant schemes and signal systemic delivery challenges.
findings.figures: Reduced from £130,000 to £80,000 (£50k cut); years 2 and 3 £500,000 each
findings.quote: The first-year allocation has been reduced due to delays in procurement, therefore DESNZ and MZNH agreed that a reduced allocation of £80,000 was more appropriate to avoid underspends at 31 st March 2026. This could be reduced further if delivery is delayed.

findings.paper_title: 3. Capital Programme Update Quarter 3 March Council meeting
findings.headline: Council's S.151 Officer states borrowing for future capital is not affordable or sustainable given medium-term revenue position
findings.detail: The Director of Resources explicitly states that while borrowing for capital schemes is theoretically possible, 'the resulting borrowing costs are unlikely to be affordable and sustainable for the revenue account, given the Council's medium-term financial position.' This signals that revenue finances are already constrained and that additional debt service cannot easily be accommodated.
findings.matters: This is a direct statement from the finance officer to the council that additional debt servicing would strain the revenue budget, signalling constrained financial headroom for a lender considering exposure to the council.
findings.figures: No specific gap quantified
findings.quote: The Council could, of course, consider borrowing for future capital schemes but the resulting borrowing costs are unlikely to be affordable and sustainable for the revenue account, given the Council's medium-term financial position (unless the capital investment generates a sufficient return).

findings.paper_title: 3. Capital Programme Update Quarter 3 March Council meeting
findings.headline: Major project (Bakewell Road Matlock, £1.02m) placed under review with no clear approval pathway
findings.detail: Project 625 totalling £1,023,339 is stated as 'currently under review' with no approval to proceed. A future Council report will be presented but no timescale is given. This represents over 5% of the total five-year capital programme now in limbo.
findings.matters: A lender needs visibility of the council's capital delivery pipeline and strategic commitments. When a major project becomes undefined, it signals either strategic uncertainty or delivery challenges that could affect the council's economic development and housing objectives.
findings.quote: Project 625 Bakewell Road, Matlock development £1,023,339. The project is currently under review. A report will be presented to a future Council meeting.

findings.paper_title: 3. Capital Programme Update Quarter 3 March Council meeting
findings.headline: £1.79m of capital schemes reprofiled out of 2025/26 due to delays and execution challenges
findings.detail: Significant capital slippage has pushed spending from 2025/26 into future years. Multiple projects are delayed: cemetery paths, parks paths, recreation ground footbridge, sewer site, and others. Notes indicate phasing reviews ongoing and works not commencing until summer/autumn 2026 or later, suggesting delivery capacity constraints.
findings.matters: Capital slippage of this magnitude signals execution or resource challenges in the council's project delivery, which affects credibility of future capital forecasts and the reliability of the programme.
findings.figures: £1,789,542 total reprofiling; largest items: Bakewell Road £1,023,339, Youlgrave PDRHA £180,000, solar panels £80,000
findings.quote: Reprofiling of schemes into 2026/27 totals £1,789,542

findings.paper_title: 3. Capital Programme Update Quarter 3 March Council meeting
findings.headline: Available capital funding depleting from £17.8m to £7.4m over five years with only £300k for new schemes after 2026
findings.detail: The council's capital receipts and discretionary reserves will decline sharply over the forecast period. The Director of Resources explicitly states that available funding for new capital schemes—excluding earmarked housing receipts—will fall to approximately £300,000. This is identified as a high-risk position for funding future capital investment.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether the council can sustain essential capital maintenance and investment when discretionary funding becomes exhausted.
findings.figures: Opening capital funding £17.8m at 1st April 2025; forecast to £7.4m by 31st March 2030. Available for new schemes only circa £300k.
findings.quote: sources of capital funding are forecast to reduce from £17.8m at 1st April 2025 to £7.4m by 31st March 2030. However, the amount available (excluding earmarked housing receipts) in the capital receipts reserve and the capital programme reserve after funding this programme is forecast to reduce to around £300,000. This presents a high risk in terms of funding availability for future projects.

findings.headline: Council holds three retail investment properties designated for yield, constraining future PWLB access
findings.detail: The council owns three retail sites acquired via ground leases in 1974, which are formally classified as investment properties held primarily to generate profit. While no borrowing was used to acquire them, PWLB rules introduced in 2021 prevent local authorities with any yield-generating assets in their capital programme from accessing PWLB borrowing. This creates a constraint on future capital funding options if the council ever needs to borrow.
findings.matters: The presence of yield assets in the portfolio—even unfunded—could lock the council out of PWLB borrowing if capital needs emerge. This limits future funding options precisely when capital receipts are dwindling.
findings.figures: 3 retail sites; acquired 1974
findings.quote: The Council has 3 retail sites which were acquired via ground leases in 1974 and are within the Council's boundary. These have been determined as investment properties for accounting purposes and are held primarily to generate a profit, although it may also be argued that the sites do contribute to the economy of the area. No borrowing has been undertaken to acquire an interest in these sites.

findings.headline: Council may need to borrow for climate net-zero projects if external funding not secured
findings.detail: The council has committed to being net zero in respect of its own emissions by 2030, but acknowledges that 'the lack of certainty in respect of funding for future years makes planning for the delivery of longer-term climate change projects challenging.' The council explicitly states that without external funding and given depleting capital receipts and reserves, it may need to consider internal or external borrowing for future capital programme updates to meet its net zero target.
findings.matters: This signals potential future borrowing pressure to meet climate commitments. If funding gaps emerge, the council may need to borrow at a time when its capital receipts are exhausted and reserves depleted, reducing negotiating position.
findings.figures: Net zero target: 2030 for council's own emissions
findings.quote: Without external funding, and with the Council's depleting capital receipts and reserves, it may be necessary to consider borrowing (internal or external) for future updates of the Capital Programme to achieve the Council's objectives in this respect.

findings.headline: Treasury investment balance shrinking from £34.2m to £14m, reducing cash resilience
findings.detail: As of 31 December 2025, the council holds £34.2m in treasury investments earning 3.86% average return. This is forecast to drop sharply to £14m by 31 March 2026—a 59% reduction in a single year. This significantly reduces the council's financial buffer for managing cash flow variations and unexpected costs.
findings.matters: Declining investment balances reduce the council's ability to absorb financial shocks or manage timing mismatches between spending and income. A tightening liquidity position constrains financial flexibility during emergencies.
findings.figures: Treasury investments: £34.2m (31.12.25) reducing to £14m (31.03.26); average return 3.86%
findings.quote: Due to decisions in the past, the Authority currently (31.12.25) has £5.45m of borrowing (at an average interest rate of 4.1%) and £34.2m of treasury investments (at an average interest rate of 3.86%). The investments are expected to reduce to £14m by 31 March 2026.

findings.headline: Council moves into technical overborrowed position from 2025/26, with gross debt exceeding CFR
findings.detail: From 2025/26 onwards, the council's gross debt is forecast to exceed its Capital Financing Requirement—gross debt of £7.56m against CFR of £7.48m, widening through the forecast period. The council acknowledges this overborrowed position but states it would not be prudent to repay the £5.45m maturity loan due in 2056 because high early settlement penalties would be charged to revenue.
findings.matters: An overborrowed position limits financial flexibility and signals constrained debt management options. Even though the council is not taking action, being locked into long-term debt due to penalty costs reduces future options.
findings.figures: 2025/26: gross debt £7,562k vs CFR £7,480k; 2026/27: £7,499k vs £7,304k. Loan: £5.45m maturity in 2056 at 4.1% average rate
findings.quote: The information in table 6 shows that from 2025/26 the Council's gross debt is forecast to be higher than the CFR which indicates that the Council is in an over borrowed position and could potentially repay some of the loan. High Premiums are imposed for settling debt before it is due which are charged to the revenue budget. At this point in time, it would not be prudent to repay any previous borrowings.

findings.headline: Capital receipts collapse from £1.2m to zero, removing a key source of capital funding
findings.detail: The council's capital receipts are forecast to plummet from £1.2m in 2025/26 to £50k in 2026/27 and zero thereafter. This is driven by declining income from the Right to Buy Sharing Agreement related to the 2002 housing stock transfer. Without capital receipts, the council loses both a funding source for capital spending and a mechanism to reduce borrowing debt.
findings.matters: A council reliant on declining capital receipts faces structural funding constraints. This forces increased dependence on reserves and grants, reducing financial flexibility for future capital investment.
findings.figures: Capital receipts: 2025/26 £1,205k; 2026/27 £50k; 2027/28 onwards £0
findings.quote: Capital receipts are dwindling as income from the Right to Buy Sharing Agreement (relating to the housing stock transfer in 2002) has reduced.

findings.headline: Council tax base is contracting, not growing; down from 31,769.90 to 31,723.67 despite government assumptions of growth from new homes.
findings.detail: The council tax base declined by approximately 46 properties. This contradicts the government's assumptions in the finance settlement, which assume council tax base growth from new homes. A shrinking tax base compounds the revenue pressure, as council tax increases apply to a smaller base.
findings.matters: A contracting tax base signals either economic weakness or a mismatch between expected development and actual uptake. It is also contrary to the government's forecast and reduces the upside from council tax increases.
findings.figures: Council Tax Base: 31,769.90 in 2025/26; 31,723.67 in 2026/27—a reduction of 46.23
findings.quote: However, it should be noted that there has been a slight reduction in the council tax base (mainly due to a change in the number of second homes).

findings.headline: Balance sheet now structurally dependent on reserve drawdowns; 2026/27 uses £1.24m from reserves to support budget, with further draws forecast.
findings.detail: The proposed budget for 2026/27 is balanced by transferring £1,238,369 from reserves to fund the business rates fluctuations reserve and support the overall budget. The Director notes this is justified as 'exceptional circumstances' due to the late settlement announcement and material impact of the Fair Funding Review and business rates reset. However, she also explicitly warns that reliance on reserves is not sustainable over the medium term.
findings.matters: Using reserves to fund recurring expenditure is inherently unsustainable. Once reserves are exhausted, the council will face either severe service cuts or a financial emergency. The council is already accepting this trade-off for 2026/27.
findings.figures: Transfers from reserves to support overall budget in 2026/27: £1,238,369; general reserve forecast at 31 March 2027: £2,485,900
findings.quote: Members must, however, note the Section 151 Officer's advice that reliance on reserves is not sustainable over the medium term, and that the Council will need to identify further savings and/or income from 2027/28 onwards to remain financially resilient.

findings.headline: Waste fleet replacement in approximately two years will require £3.6m; current reserve provision is only £1.5m, leaving a £2.1m funding gap.
findings.detail: The current waste vehicle fleet was acquired in 2020/21 and 2021/22 at a cost of £3.6m. These vehicles will require replacement around 2028/29, or the council will face increased annual revenue costs if vehicles are leased instead. The Waste Vehicles Reserve is forecast to have only £1.5m by March 2027, leaving a material shortfall. The Director of Resources notes this as a risk that could add to budget pressures already identified in the MTFP.
findings.matters: This is a known, approaching liability for which the council is underprovided. It will create either a capital requirement or a permanent increase in revenue expenditure from 2028/29 onwards, precisely when the council faces the largest budget gap.
findings.figures: Waste vehicles cost 2020/21 and 2021/22: £3.6m; Waste Vehicles Reserve forecast at 31 March 2027: £1,500,000
findings.quote: In addition to the above, there is a need to build up a reserve to be utilised when the Council's current fleet of waste vehicles require replacement in 2 years' time, or to plan for increased annual revenue costs at the end of the current contract if future vehicles are to be leased.

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation costs remain unquantified; £50k budgeted for project management only, despite case for change suggesting £17m pre-vesting costs across Derbyshire.
findings.detail: Vesting day is April 2028. The council has budgeted only £50,000 for LGR project management costs in 2026/27, and no provision for implementation or transition costs in 2026/27 or 2027/28. However, the case for change from other Derbyshire authorities estimates total pre-vesting costs at £17m. The government expects existing councils to fund this. The actual financial requirements depend on the ministerial decision and shadow authority decisions—currently unknown.
findings.matters: This is a material contingent liability that could force significant additional spending in 2026/27 and 2027/28 with no current budget provision. The £17m estimate suggests the council's actual contribution could be substantial.
findings.figures: £50,000 for LGR project management in 2026/27; other Derbyshire authorities' case for change indicates £17 million total pre-vesting costs
findings.quote: At this point, the Council has not set aside financial provision for LGR beyond £50,000 on the 2026/27 revenue budget for project management costs. This is due to the current uncertainty around the timing and scale of required contributions.

findings.headline: Massive impact from business rates baseline reset: retained business rates income cut from £4.3m to £1.7m in a single year.
findings.detail: The 2026/27 finance settlement included a full reset of the business rates baseline. This removed £2.6m of business rates income that the council had been retaining above the baseline. This is not a forecast risk—it is already embedded in the 2026/27 figures and reflects structural loss of income.
findings.matters: This is a permanent structural reduction in the council's revenue base, not a temporary shortfall. It cannot be recovered and demonstrates the volatility of business rates-dependent funding.
findings.figures: Retained Business Rates (NDR): £4,318,598 in 2025/26 original budget; £1,713,160 in 2026/27 proposed budget—a reduction of £2,605,438
findings.quote: The Reset of the Business Rates Baseline is a technical exercise to update the government's assessment of: how much business rates are available (updating Business Rates Baselines); and where they are needed (updating Baseline Funding Levels). The outcome is a change in the Council's retained share of business rates income.

findings.headline: Strategic reserves are depleting at a faster rate than comparable authorities, dropping from £16.9m to £8.5m in two years to fund services and balance deficits.
findings.detail: Total strategic reserves and balances will fall by 49% in just two years (March 2025 to March 2027). The CIPFA Financial Resilience Index flags the council as higher-risk for 'Change In Reserves', indicating reserves are being drawn down faster than similar councils. The Director of Resources explicitly states higher levels of reserves are required in the medium-term.
findings.matters: Rapid reserve depletion signals financial stress and reduces the council's ability to respond to unexpected pressures or opportunities. It is also not sustainable for funding ongoing expenditure.
findings.figures: Strategic reserves: £16.9m at 31 March 2025; forecast £12.3m at 31 March 2026; forecast £8.5m at 31 March 2027
findings.quote: Following this review of reserves, strategic reserves are estimated to total £12.3 million at 31st March 2026, reducing to £8.5 million at 31st March 2027.

findings.headline: Council is critically dependent on a £820,000 Extended Producer Responsibility grant that may not be available or could reduce significantly in future years.
findings.detail: This single grant is a material factor in balancing the 2026/27 budget. The council explicitly assessed it as a high financial risk, with the MTFP assuming it reduces to zero over 2026/27 to 2029/30. Without it, the 2026/27 budget would have required finding an additional £820k from other sources. Loss of this grant would immediately create a major shortfall.
findings.matters: A lender cannot rely on forecast income streams that the council itself assesses as high-risk and non-recurring. This is a cliff risk if the government withdraws or reduces the grant.
findings.figures: £820,000 in 2026/27, forecast to reduce to zero by 2029/30
findings.quote: There is a high financial risk that this grant may not be available in future years or that it will reduce significantly. The MTFP assumes that it will reduce to zero over the period 2026/27 to 2029/30.

findings.headline: Structural budget cliff edge arrives in 2029/30 when transitional government funding protections end, with savings requirements escalating from £732k to £4.2m annually.
findings.detail: The council faces escalating budget gaps if it cannot identify savings: £732,000 in 2027/28, £2.8m in 2028/29, and £4.2m in 2029/30. The Director explicitly flags this as a high financial risk. After 2028/29 there is no confirmation that transitional funding arrangements will continue, and no assumptions can be made at this stage about government support beyond the three-year settlement.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether a council can actually achieve £4m+ in annual savings, and what happens if it cannot. This is not a forward-looking pressure—it is built into the current settlement.
findings.quote: There is concern that we will face a "cliff edge" after 2028/29 when the protections are due to end unless we are able to make savings to offset the loss of protections. This should be noted as a high financial risk.

findings.headline: Council faces simultaneous pressures on both revenue budget and capital resources
findings.detail: The Asset Management Plan is framed as a tool to manage these dual financial pressures. The council expects the plan to create opportunities to maximise value from land and buildings, identify costs and investment needs for specific assets, and identify financial opportunities that support environmental sustainability. The financial risk of the plan itself is assessed as low.
findings.matters: Dual-axis financial stress on both revenue and capital is a material indicator for lending decisions; it suggests the council may need to rely on asset disposals or restrictions on capital spending to manage cash
findings.figures: None specific
findings.quote: The Council currently faces pressures on both its revenue budget and its capital resources.

findings.headline: Draft financial statements published 8 August 2025, over a month after the 30 June statutory deadline
findings.detail: The 2024/25 draft accounts were published on 8 August 2025, missing the statutory deadline by 39 days. The council prioritized quality over timeliness, citing internal resource challenges and implementation of new accounting standard IFRS 16. The auditor notes this requires further improvement in 2025/26.
findings.matters: Late publication of draft accounts indicates finance team resource constraints or process gaps, and signals timing pressure during final closedown. This could mask underlying issues in financial close capability.
findings.figures: Published 8 August 2025 vs 30 June statutory deadline
findings.quote: further improvements in the closedown timetable are necessary in 2025/26 to produce draft financial statements by the statutory deadline

findings.headline: MTFP identifies £9.5m in required savings or additional income over the forecast period, with £1.3m needed for 2026/27
findings.detail: The Medium Term Financial Plan identifies future funding gaps requiring £1.3m in savings for 2026/27 (reduced from an originally identified £2.6m in March 2024 MTFP), and £9.5m total savings or income generation across the MTFP lifetime.
findings.matters: This quantifies the council's structural challenge and the scale of rebalancing required. While the council has a strong track record of delivery and underspends, this represents a multi-year savings programme that must be sustained.
findings.figures: £1.3m required for 2026/27, £9.5m total over MTFP lifetime, originally £2.6m target in March 2024
findings.quote: the Council has identified a need to make savings or generate additional income of £9.5m which will require a continued focus on the strong financial management arrangements in place over recent years

findings.headline: Earmarked reserves depleting over time while being drawn down to fund service delivery, which auditor flags as unsustainable
findings.detail: Earmarked reserves have declined from £20.9m in 2021 to £16.9m in 2025, reflecting planned use to support service delivery and capital projects. The auditor explicitly states this trend is 'not a sustainable approach' and that 'future financial plans will require continued strong monitoring to ensure reserves remain sufficient for the medium term.'
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the sustainability of the council's financial cushion. Systematic depletion of reserves to fund ongoing service delivery signals a structural funding gap that cannot continue indefinitely.
findings.figures: Earmarked reserves £20.9m (2021) to £16.9m (2025), total useable reserves decreased by £0.3m (1%) in 2024/25 despite £2.6m underspend
findings.quote: the use of reserves to support service delivery is not a sustainable approach, and future financial plans will require continued strong monitoring to ensure reserves remain sufficient for the medium term

findings.paper_title: Fees and Charges Report for 2026-27 For G&R 08-11-2026
findings.headline: Land Charges service anticipated to lose income following migration to Land Registry
findings.detail: The Local Land Charges service is migrating to the Land Registry with completion due 'within the foreseeable future', which is anticipated to result in income loss. This follows the experience in 2025/26 when the council raised Land Charges fees (Non-Vatable by 4%, Vatable by 9%), but demand fell significantly, resulting in overall income reduction rather than increase, prompting the council to freeze fees.
findings.matters: Lenders need visibility on anticipated revenue stream losses and evidence that the council faces demand elasticity constraints when raising service fees, affecting its ability to self-fund services.
findings.figures: Non-Vatable +4%, Vatable +9% in 2025/26; resulted in overall income reduction; migration timing not specified beyond 'foreseeable future'
findings.quote: A price increase in 2025/26 of Non-Vatable (4%) and Vatable (9%) resulted in a change in the demand dynamics of land charges in the current year, effectively resulting in an overall reduction in income for the Council.

findings.headline: Designation requires Council to maintain administrative costs for Secretary of State applications despite losing fee income
findings.detail: Even if designated, the Council retains administrative responsibilities for major applications submitted directly to the Planning Inspectorate under Section 62A. This means the Council continues to incur costs for processing and administration while losing associated planning application fees, creating a net negative financial position.
findings.matters: The Council faces costs without corresponding revenue, creating financial pressure and budget headroom reduction at a time of wider fiscal pressure
findings.figures: None quantified in the paper
findings.quote: It is important to note that the Council would retain a key administrative role in relation to applications submitted under Section 62A meaning that they would still represent a significant cost commitment to the Council, despite the associated loss of fee income.

findings.headline: Designation would exacerbate an already critical planning staff recruitment shortage
findings.detail: Councils that have undergone designation report significant adverse impacts on staff morale and increased difficulties recruiting professional planning staff. The planning sector faces a long-term acute nationwide shortage. Designation would worsen this for Derbyshire Dales, risking departures of experienced staff at a time when the Council is managing recent appointments of three senior planning officers and two graduate trainees.
findings.matters: Loss of planning expertise and higher staff turnover increases operational risk and reduces the council's capacity to manage complex applications and implement its development strategy
findings.figures: None provided for Derbyshire Dales specifically; impact estimated from other designated councils' experience
findings.quote: Councils which have undergone designation report significant adverse impacts on staff morale coupled with increased difficulties in recruiting new staff to the planning service. The current recruitment climate for professional planning staff is already extremely challenging due to a long-term acute nationwide shortage of planners.

findings.headline: The Council's 1.36-year housing land supply creates planning policy pressure independent of designation
findings.detail: The Council's housing supply for 2024-2029 is only 1.36 years, well below the five-year requirement. This triggers the 'tilted balance' in planning law that favors development and shifts planning considerations in favor of housing delivery. This creates a structural incentive for developers to submit applications directly to the Planning Inspectorate, occurring whether or not formal designation happens.
findings.matters: A critically short housing supply means the Council loses control over major development decisions as developers exploit the tilted balance by bypassing the LPA and going direct to the Secretary of State
findings.figures: 1.36 years housing supply for 2024-2029 period
findings.quote: the Council's supply of housing from 1 st April 2024 to 31st March 2029 stands at 1.36 years meaning that the so called 'tilted balance' set out in paragraph 11 of the National Planning Policy Framework is invoked. This significantly shifts the balance of planning considerations in favour of housing delivery.

findings.headline: One outstanding appeal decision by end of 2025 could trigger designation by exceeding the 10% rejection threshold
findings.detail: The Council's current appeal rejection rate is 9.8%, just 0.2% below the 10% threshold for designation. A single appeal on Land at Throstle Nest Way is pending decision by end of 2025. If allowed, the Council's performance would rise to 11.76%, triggering designation. The Secretary of State's designation decision is expected early 2026.
findings.matters: Designation is a material operational and financial event that fundamentally changes how the council operates and reduces its fee income within months
findings.figures: 9.8% current rate; 10% threshold; 0.2% margin; 11.76% if one appeal allowed
findings.quote: Performance to date stands just 0.2% below the threshold at 9.8% with only one appeal decision outstanding relating to Land at Throstle Nest Way, Brailsford. If the appeal is allowed, the Council's performance will stand above the 10% threshold at 11.76%.

findings.headline: Designation could result in loss of £200,000 to £250,000 in annual planning fee income
findings.detail: Major applications currently account for approximately half of the Council's £400,000 to £500,000 total planning application fee income. If designated, most major applications would be submitted directly to the Planning Inspectorate, bypassing the Council. In a worst-case scenario, this represents a material loss to the Council's revenue base.
findings.matters: A loss of £200-250k annually represents a significant reduction in the council's revenue base affecting its financial sustainability and borrowing capacity
findings.figures: £200,000 to £250,000 each year; currently fees for major applications account for approximately half of the annual £400,000 to £500,000 total planning application fee income
findings.quote: In a worst case scenario, designation could therefore result in a loss of fee income of approximately £200,000 to £250,000 each year.

findings.headline: Significant unbudgeted repairs at Town Hall, depots and riverbank
findings.detail: Repairs and maintenance budget exceeded by £66k due to significant unforeseen work at the Town Hall, Northwood Depot, and Bakewell riverbank. The report acknowledges 'the repairs and maintenance budget is a reactive one and further review of this budget is to take place to ensure adequate budget resource is allocated.'
findings.matters: This signals a maintenance backlog and indicates the current budget allocation is insufficient for the council's estate, suggesting deferred maintenance issues.
findings.figures: £66k overspend in 2025/26; budget noted as under-resourced
findings.quote: The repairs and maintenance budget is forecast to exceed budget by £66k as a result of significant unforeseen repair and maintenance work at numerous locations across the District, including the Town Hall, Northwood Depot and Bakewell riverbank. It is acknowledged that the repairs and maintenance budget is a reactive one and further review of this budget is to take place to ensure adequate budget resource is allocated.

findings.headline: Escalating corporate savings targets of £1.7m to £3.7m in years 2027-2030
findings.detail: The MTFP shows the council must find cumulative savings of £1,655k (2027/28), £2,594k (2028/29), and £3,673k (2029/30). These are growing annual targets that must be delivered against a background of structural income losses.
findings.matters: The council must identify and deliver increasingly large spending cuts. The trajectory suggests either significant service reductions or unsustainable reserve drawdowns will be needed.

findings.headline: Waste recycling credits down £59k on permanent structural basis
findings.detail: Recycling credit income is forecast to reduce by £59k due to lower waste material market prices. This is treated as an ongoing structural reduction and built into the 2026/27 budget.
findings.matters: Another permanent income reduction that compounds financial pressures. The council cannot control commodity market prices, making this a structural vulnerability.
findings.figures: £59k reduction in 2025/26; ongoing from 2026/27 onwards
findings.quote: It is anticipated that income received for dry recycling credits will be reduced by approximately £59k as a result of the current material market, which has led to lower rebates. This is considered to be an on-going reduction and therefore this pressure has been built into the 2026/27 budget setting process.

findings.headline: Permanent car parking income reduction from free parking policy
findings.detail: Car parking income is £49k below budget in 2025/26 due to the 30 minutes free parking policy implemented from April 2025 and the Ashbourne Reborn project. This is treated as a permanent structural loss and built into the 2026/27 budget.
findings.matters: Policy decisions that reduce income compound the council's need to find escalating savings. This reduction is permanent, not a one-off timing issue.
findings.figures: £49k underspend in 2025/26; permanent loss from 2026/27 onwards
findings.quote: Car parking income is currently forecast to underachieve budget by £49k, this is mainly due to the impacts of the 30 minutes free parking implemented from 1 April 2025 and the Ashbourne Reborn project. This pressure is anticipated to be a permanent reduction in car parking income and therefore has been included in the updated medium term financial plan.

findings.headline: Local government reorganisation cost impact cannot be quantified
findings.detail: The MTFP excludes 'the impact of Local Government Re-organisation, the potential additional cost of which cannot currently be quantified.' This is a material gap in financial planning.
findings.matters: Structural local government changes could impose significant unforeseen costs at an unpredictable time, and the council cannot currently assess the impact.
findings.figures: Cost cannot be quantified
findings.quote: the impact of Local Government Re-organisation, the potential additional cost of which cannot currently be quantified

findings.headline: Waste and leisure contract renewals in 2028/29 with unquantified costs
findings.detail: The MTFP explicitly excludes costing for both waste and leisure services contracts, which expire in 2028/29 and are due for renewal. The council states it cannot quantify the potential cost impact. This represents a major unknown liability in the medium term.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the scale of these contract renewals and their funding impact before that year arrives, as they could materially worsen the council's financial position.
findings.figures: Contracts expire 2028/29; costs unquantified
findings.quote: The current MTFP does not include any potential significant additional budget pressures relating to expenditure on the waste and leisure contracts which are both due to expire in 2028/29

findings.paper_title: 10. Treasury Management Outturn 2024-25 and Mid-Year 2025-26 Report
findings.headline: Council maintains £140,000 reserve for pooled fund accounting risk pending regulatory clarity
findings.detail: The council set up a reserve of £140,000 to mitigate the impact if the statutory override on accounting gains and losses in pooled investment funds (held until 1 April 2029) is not extended. The council has decided to maintain this reserve given regulatory uncertainty.
findings.matters: Shows prudent management of accounting and regulatory risk on a £0.9m pooled property fund investment; demonstrates forward-looking financial governance.
findings.figures: £140,000 reserve; £0.9m CCLA pooled property fund investment
findings.quote: the Authority has decided to maintain this reserve for the time being.

findings.paper_title: 10. Treasury Management Outturn 2024-25 and Mid-Year 2025-26 Report
findings.headline: IFRS 16 finance lease accounting effective 2024-25 adds £2.2m to reported debt position
findings.detail: New accounting treatment for finance leases (IFRS 16, effective from 2024-25) adds £2.2m to the Capital Financing Requirement. This accounting change affects how the council's leverage is measured compared to prior years but does not reflect new cash borrowing.
findings.matters: Changes in accounting standards affect reported debt levels and leverage metrics; lenders need to adjust comparisons year-on-year and understand the impact on creditworthiness assessment.
findings.figures: £2.2m finance lease liability in 2024-25 and forecast 2025-26
findings.quote: Less IFRS 16 – Finance Leases* N/A (2.2) (2.2) [*effective from 2024/25]

findings.paper_title: 10. Treasury Management Outturn 2024-25 and Mid-Year 2025-26 Report
findings.headline: Council moved to overborrowed position, providing liquidity to repay debt early if needed
findings.detail: Derbyshire Dales moved from underborrowed (£0.1m at 31/3/24) to overborrowed in 2024-25 and forecast to remain so. With treasury investments of £21.5m (31/3/25) and £34.2m (30/9/25) against a capital financing requirement of £7.7m and external borrowing of only £5.5m, the council has substantial liquidity.
findings.matters: Overborrowed position signals strong debt servicing capacity and financial flexibility; lenders assess this as demonstrating ability to meet obligations under stress.
findings.figures: Capital financing requirement £7.7m; external borrowing £5.5m; treasury investments £34.2m (30/9/25)
findings.quote: the council will be in an overborrowed position, which indicates that if no new borrowing is required, the Council could repay debt early.

findings.paper_title: 10. Treasury Management Outturn 2024-25 and Mid-Year 2025-26 Report
findings.headline: Investment income exceeded budget by £810,760 in 2024-25, with 2025-26 forecast to outperform again
findings.detail: The council earned £1,331,660 in treasury investment income against a budget of £520,900 in 2024-25. For 2025-26, income is forecast at £1,000,000 against a budget of £736,177. This outperformance improves the revenue budget and demonstrates effective cash management.
findings.matters: Strong investment returns show the council's ability to manage substantial cash balances (£21.5m–£34.2m) effectively and provide budget flexibility; important to lenders assessing financial management capability.
findings.quote: Actual Investment Income earned in 2024/25 was £1,331,66 against a budget of £520,900.

news_drafts.headline: Ashbourne Reborn regeneration project carries high assessed risk despite being on track
news_drafts.lead: A £15.2m capital scheme that is the council's responsibility as Accountable Body carries concentration risk. High assessed risk means the council has identified material things that could go wrong. If the project slips or faces cost overruns, it could…

news_drafts.headline: Monitoring Officer resigned during 2025/26; recruitment ongoing with interim arrangements in place
news_drafts.lead: The Monitoring Officer role is critical to ensuring the council operates within law and maintains governance standards. A vacant statutory post creates execution risk on compliance and ethics oversight. The longer the interim period, the greater the…

news_drafts.headline: Council tax and business rates collection rates fell below target in 2025/26, driven by cost of living crisis
news_drafts.lead: Collection rates directly affect the income available to fund services and close the budget gap. Falling rates in a cost-of-living crisis environment suggest the underlying trend may worsen before it improves, worsening the financial sustainability picture.
